title: Hyperkinetic Movement Disorders and Hereditary Ataxias

steps.tx: An autosomal dominant, fully penetrant progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterised by the clinical triad of involuntary choreiform movements, psychiatric and behavioural disturbances, and relentless cognitive decline is **Huntington disease**. Pathology features profound atrophy of the caudate nucleus and putamen (striatum) with loss of medium spiny GABAergic neurons.
steps.say: An autosomal dominant progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by involuntary choreiform movements, psychiatric disturbances, and cognitive decline is Huntington disease. Neuropathology features profound atrophy of the caudate nucleus and putamen with loss of GABAergic neurons.

steps.tx: Genetically, Huntington disease is caused by an unstable, expanded **CAG trinucleotide repeat** encoding an elongated polyglutamine tract in the huntingtin (HTT) gene on the short arm of chromosome 4. Normal alleles contain under twenty-six repeats; full disease penetrance occurs with thirty-six or more repeats, leading to toxic gain-of-function protein aggregation and nuclear neuronal death.
steps.say: Genetically, Huntington disease is caused by an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat encoding an elongated polyglutamine tract in the huntingtin gene on chromosome 4. Full disease penetrance occurs with thirty-six or more repeats, leading to toxic gain-of-function protein aggregation.

steps.tx: Trinucleotide repeat instability during gametogenesis explains the phenomenon of genetic **anticipation**, wherein subsequent generations manifest earlier disease onset and more severe clinical symptoms. In Huntington disease, anticipation occurs predominantly during paternal spermatogenesis, where massive repeat expansions can precipitate juvenile Huntington disease (Westphal variant) presenting with rigid hypokinetic parkinsonism.
steps.say: Trinucleotide repeat instability during gametogenesis explains genetic anticipation, wherein subsequent generations manifest earlier disease onset and more severe symptoms. In Huntington disease, anticipation occurs predominantly during paternal transmission, precipitating juvenile rigid parkinsonism.

steps.tx: The signature hyperkinetic motor abnormality of Huntington disease is **chorea**, characterised by rapid, involuntary, non-rhythmic, jerky, purposeless, migratory movements that flow irregularly from one muscle group to another. Patients frequently attempt to mask these movements by incorporating them into semi-purposeful gestures (parakinesia) and display motor impersistence (milkmaid grip, tongue darting).
steps.say: The signature hyperkinetic motor abnormality of Huntington disease is chorea, characterized by rapid, involuntary, non-rhythmic, purposeless migratory movements flowing irregularly between muscle groups. Patients frequently incorporate them into semi-purposeful gestures, accompanied by motor impersistence.

steps.tx: Involuntary, sustained or intermittent muscle contractions causing twisting and repetitive movements or abnormal postures are classified as **dystonia**. Examples include focal cervical dystonia (spasmodic torticollis), blepharospasm, writer cramp, and generalized dystonias. First-line therapy for disabling focal dystonias is local intramuscular injection of botulinum toxin to block neuromuscular acetylcholine release.

Examples include cervical torticollis, blepharospasm, and writer cramp. First-line therapy for disabling focal dystonias is local intramuscular injection of botulinum neurotoxin.

steps.tx: The most common autosomal recessive hereditary ataxia in clinical practice is **Friedreich ataxia**. Caused by an expanded non-coding intronic GAA trinucleotide repeat in the FXN gene on chromosome 9, it leads to severe transcriptional silencing of the mitochondrial iron-chaperone protein frataxin, triggering intra-mitochondrial iron accumulation, reactive oxygen species generation, and respiratory chain failure.
steps.say: The most common autosomal recessive hereditary ataxia is Friedreich ataxia. Caused by an expanded intronic GAA trinucleotide repeat in the frataxin gene, it leads to deficiency of mitochondrial frataxin, triggering iron accumulation, oxidative stress, and respiratory chain failure.

steps.tx: The neuropathology of Friedreich ataxia involves combined degeneration of the dorsal root ganglia, posterior columns (causing profound loss of proprioception and vibration), spinocerebellar tracts, and descending corticospinal motor tracts. Patients present before age twenty-five with progressive gait ataxia, absent deep tendon reflexes in the lower limbs, extensor Babinski responses, and pes **cavus** foot deformity with kyphoscoliosis.
steps.say: The neuropathology of Friedreich ataxia involves combined degeneration of the posterior columns, spinocerebellar tracts, and corticospinal pathways. Patients present before age twenty-five with progressive gait ataxia, absent lower limb reflexes, extensor Babinski responses, and pes cavus with kyphoscoliosis.

steps.tx: Physical examination of the motor system differentiates cerebellar from sensory ataxia. Classical **cerebellar signs** comprise kinetic intention tremor, dysmetria on finger-nose-finger testing, dysdiadochokinesia (impaired rapid alternating movements), cerebellar scanning staccato dysarthria, horizontal gaze-evoked nystagmus, and a wide-based, uncoordinated staggering gait that fails to worsen significantly with eye closure.
steps.say: Physical examination differentiates cerebellar from sensory ataxia. Classical cerebellar signs comprise intention tremor, dysmetria on finger-to-nose testing, dysdiadochokinesia, cerebellar scanning speech, horizontal nystagmus, and a wide-based staggering gait that persists with eyes open or closed.
